records.name: Moscow
records.summary:
Moscow is where the federal anti-LGBT framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution — headlined around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” — records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, Kotov, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024; the paper reported Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-‘extremism’ designation in February 2025, an organising case following a ruling reported from Siberia in January 2025.

The severity of the federal law is uniform across the country, but enforcement intensity is not: Moscow concentrates the highest police density, the most active venue-level operations, and the bureaucratic touchpoints most likely to involve a foreign visitor — document verification, medical gatekeeping, registration procedures. For a trans visitor the practical result is a materially higher probability of encountering active enforcement of the same rules, and the country offers no protective institutional counterweight at any level.

records.name: Orenburg Oblast
records.summary:
Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction where the federal "LGBT extremism" designation first produced a criminal conviction against a commercial leisure venue. The Pose bar case (submitted to court July 2025 by the regional Investigative Committee) resulted in June 2026 in a seven-year sentence for owner Vyacheslav Khasanov, prison terms for two employees, and forfeiture of over one million rubles—the first criminal LGBT-extremism sentencing against a commercial venue in Russia (the first prison sentence under the extremism designation overall was handed down by a Siberian court in an organising case, reported January 2025, predating this one). The precedent establishes that a bar or club can be prosecuted as an extremist organisation, which is the scenario a foreign visitor walking into a commercial venue is most likely to encounter.

This is visitor-facing enforcement: the venue context (drinking, socialising) is exactly where a visiting trans person might interact with the criminal justice system. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. Comparable to Moscow (0.09), which concentrates raids and the first organiser prosecution; both represent active enforcement venues within the uniform federal law. Orenburg's specific finding—a seven-year sentence against a bar owner—sets the most severe commercial-venue precedent in the country.

records.name: NCR
records.summary:
The Philippines has no national anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity; the national picture is violence against trans women, documented in a 2024–2025 series of killings, without dependable local machinery. The capital region carries the country's strongest local protections: in July 2025 Quezon City became its first local government unit to enact a Gender-Inclusive Health Ordinance, creating a framework for gender-affirming primary care, mental-health support and specialist services through the city's public-health system — the only enforceable institutional recourse a discovered visitor can find anywhere in the archipelago.

Lethal violence is on the regional record too: the transrespectful memorial lists Shaina Bayabay, 29, strangled during a drinking session in Pasig City, Metro Manila, on 1 March 2024. Protection here is real but partial — a functioning framework on paper in the country's largest city, and an enforcement-and-services reality that does not yet extend past city limits.

records.name: Central Visayas
records.summary:
Central Visayas holds the most active provincial-level anti-discrimination ordinance cluster outside the capital region. Mandaue City signed the Implementation Rules and Regulations of its Anti-Discrimination Ordinance in July 2024, formalised jointly with the city mayor, the KAABAG LGBT Federation and a UN development programme — an operational, not merely symbolic, local protection in the Cebu metro. The municipality of Carmen, northern Cebu, approved a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance protecting people on SOGIE grounds by unanimous Sangguniang Bayan vote in June 2025, days before the end of Pride month.

No killings, assaults or institutional-hostility incidents specific to trans visitors or residents are documented in this region within the 2024-2025 national violence series or elsewhere in the research record. A visitor in Cebu/Mandaue can invoke an operational anti-discrimination ordinance — protection without any accompanying regional violence signal.

records.name: Soccsksargen
records.summary:
In June 2025, transgender-rights activist Ali Jejhon Macalintal was shot dead in General Santos City. Human Rights Watch called the killing an “apparent targeted killing” and said police were examining her activism as a possible motive. The national Commission on Human Rights publicly condemned the killings of two transgender women as “marked by cruelty and impunity” — the strongest official wording in this record for any region — and named Macalintal.

No protective ordinance or institutional counterweight is documented in this region, and the killing stood unresolved as of the record's sources. For a trans visitor the finding is targeted lethal violence against activists in a province with an official acknowledgement of impunity and no local machinery to answer it.

records.name: Central Luzon
records.summary:
Angeles City and the Clark-Subic corridor in Pampanga constitute the region's principal traveler-facing risk. In June 2025 the National Bureau of Investigation's Bataan District Office dismantled a trafficking operation at Field Sensation's Bar in Angeles City, arresting four people and rescuing 45 victims including 13 minors; in March 2025 the same office arrested a foreign national and accomplices in Angeles City under the Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act, rescuing 12 victims including 5 minors. Peer-reviewed research describes the US military-basing economy around Clark as sustaining sexual markets that disproportionately exploit poor transgender Filipina women, and the 2024 US Trafficking in Persons Report confirms traffickers exploit victims in tourist destinations and urban areas around the country.

For a transgender visitor the exposure is two-fold: the venues where trans women are concentrated in commercial sex work carry the highest violence and trafficking risk, and enforcement sweeps can sweep up anyone in the vicinity. No protective ordinance cluster comparable to the capital region or Central Visayas is documented here.

records.name: Calabarzon
records.summary:
This region surrounds the national capital without sharing its protective ordinances: none is documented here, and the visitor picture is the national one — killings of trans women without dependable local machinery.

Against that backdrop, in August 2025 a newly crowned LGBTQ pageant winner was found dead with 13 stab wounds in a city south of the capital, days after the crowning, and police worked the killing as a homicide case — a high-signal violent episode for this region's record.

records.name: Cagayan Valley
records.summary: On 31 July 2024 in Ilagan City, Isabela, Morine "G." Cabansag, 40, was found dead in a cemetery after an alleged kidnapping and rape in Centro San Antonio; three suspects were identified. The monitored trans-murder count records the cause as stabbing. This is one of six documented killings of trans women in eighteen months in the national series, with arrests made in at least three of them and none reported prosecuted to conviction. No protective ordinance, institutional-hostility finding or enforcement pattern specific to trans visitors is documented in this region beyond this single incident.
